note: Lot 11 — document Word « ToxiScan Food Additive Descriptions » (81 additifs E). Badge du document = source de vérité. INDUSTRIAL -> Occasional (jaune), PROCESSED -> Processed (orange), ULTRA TOXIC -> Ultra toxic.

entries.name: patent blue v
entries.description_en: A synthetic blue dye used only to change appearance and provide no nutritional value. Current authorized uses have not been shown to create a general safety concern, but rare hypersensitivity reactions are possible. Health: People with a history of reactions to synthetic dyes should be cautious. The additive mainly signals a highly formulated product.

entries.name: green s
entries.description_en: A synthetic green food dye used to create or intensify color. It has an acceptable daily intake, and high consumption of several colored products can increase total exposure. Health: The concern is unnecessary cumulative exposure and possible intolerance in sensitive individuals, not proven carcinogenicity.

entries.name: brilliant black bn
entries.description_en: A synthetic black dye used in confectionery, sauces, decorations, and other processed foods. Some high-consuming children may approach or exceed the acceptable daily intake. Health: Frequent consumption of several products containing this dye can increase exposure beyond the level intended for daily use.

entries.name: brown ht
entries.description_en: A synthetic brown dye used in bakery, dessert, and confectionery products. Exposure estimates have indicated that some high consumers, particularly children, may exceed the acceptable daily intake. Health: The main concern is repeated high intake from multiple colored products.

entries.name: paprika extract, capsanthin and capsorubin
entries.description_en: A concentrated red-orange color extracted from paprika and processed to standardize pigment strength. It is not considered a high-risk additive at permitted levels. Health: Quality control is important for solvent residues and purity. Rare paprika-related allergic reactions may occur in sensitive people.

entries.name: canthaxanthin
entries.description_en: An orange-red carotenoid color with a low acceptable daily intake. Excessive exposure can cause canthaxanthin crystals to accumulate in the retina. Health: High intake may produce retinal deposits and visual changes. This is a genuine dose-related health concern and is why use is tightly restricted.

entries.name: calcium sorbate
entries.description_en: A former preservative used to slow mold and yeast growth. It was withdrawn from the European Union food-additive list because the available data were insufficient to rule out a genotoxic concern. Health: Avoid products that list it as a food additive in markets where it is not authorized. Withdrawal reflects unresolved safety data, not proof that it causes cancer.

entries.name: calcium benzoate
entries.description_en: A synthetic preservative that releases benzoate to slow microbial growth in acidic foods and drinks. It adds to total exposure from benzoic acid and other benzoates. Health: Sensitive individuals may experience hives or asthma-like reactions. High combined exposure should remain below the acceptable daily intake.

entries.name: ethyl paraben
entries.description_en: A synthetic paraben preservative used to prevent mold and bacterial growth. Experimental research has examined weak hormone-like activity, so exposure is controlled through a combined acceptable daily intake. Health: No cancer claim is justified at authorized food levels. The relevant concern is repeated combined exposure to several parabens.

entries.name: sodium ethyl paraben
entries.description_en: The water-soluble sodium form of ethyl paraben. It is an industrial antimicrobial preservative and contributes to the same combined paraben exposure limit as ethyl paraben. Health: The main concern is cumulative exposure to parabens rather than an immediate toxic effect at permitted levels.

entries.name: propyl paraben
entries.description_en: A paraben preservative that is no longer authorized as a food additive in the European Union. Regulators could not establish an acceptable daily intake from the available reproductive-toxicity data. Health: The unresolved concern involves possible reproductive effects at sufficient exposure. Non-authorization does not prove that ordinary trace exposure causes cancer.

entries.name: sodium propyl paraben
entries.description_en: The sodium form of propyl paraben, also no longer authorized as a food additive in the European Union. Its safety could not be adequately confirmed from the available reproductive-toxicity evidence. Health: Avoid as a declared food additive where it is not authorized. The concern is insufficient safety assurance, especially for repeated exposure.

entries.name: methyl paraben
entries.description_en: A synthetic preservative used against molds and bacteria. It has weak biological activity in laboratory testing, but food use is regulated under a combined acceptable daily intake with ethyl paraben. Health: The practical concern is cumulative exposure from food, medicines, and personal-care products, not proven cancer from permitted food levels.

entries.name: sodium methyl paraben
entries.description_en: The sodium salt of methyl paraben, designed to dissolve more easily in water. It is a synthetic preservative counted within the same combined exposure limit as methyl and ethyl parabens. Health: Repeated exposure from several sources is more relevant than a single food serving.

entries.name: soybean hemicellulose
entries.description_en: A processed fiber fraction extracted from soybeans and used to thicken, stabilize, or keep particles suspended. It is mainly an industrial texture ingredient. Health: Residual soy proteins may matter for people with a severe soy allergy, even though the additive itself is not considered highly toxic.

entries.name: beta-cyclodextrin
entries.description_en: A ring-shaped carbohydrate manufactured from starch and used to trap, protect, or carry flavors and other compounds. It has a relatively low acceptable daily intake. Health: High exposure can exceed the recommended daily limit. The restriction is based on systemic effects observed at higher doses, not on a cancer classification.

entries.name: tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
entries.description_en: Chemically modified fats used to strengthen dough, stabilize mixtures, and control texture. They are characteristic of industrial bakery and processed-food formulations. Health: No major specific disease risk is established at authorized levels. The relevant concern is cumulative intake and manufacturing impurities.
keywords: tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
esters tartriques de mono- et diglycérides
esters tartriques de mono et diglycerides
tartaric acid esters of mono and diglycerides

entries.name: mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
entries.description_en: A complex emulsifier made by chemically esterifying mono- and diglycerides. It improves dough performance, volume, and shelf stability in industrial foods. Health: No carcinogenic classification applies. Purity, total tartaric-acid exposure, and frequent consumption of heavily formulated foods are the main considerations.
keywords: mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
esters acétiques et tartriques de mono- et diglycérides
esters acetiques et tartriques de mono et diglycerides
mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono and diglycerides

entries.name: sucroglycerides
entries.description_en: Industrial emulsifiers produced by reacting sucrose with food fats. They help oil and water remain mixed and create a stable, smooth texture in highly formulated foods. Health: Some exposure scenarios may approach or exceed the group acceptable daily intake. Large amounts may also contribute to digestive discomfort.

entries.name: potassium carbonates
entries.description_en: Refined mineral salts used to control acidity, improve dough, or support manufacturing. They are not considered harmful at normal food levels. Health: Very high potassium intake can be dangerous for people with kidney disease or those taking medicines that raise blood potassium.

entries.name: ammonium carbonates
entries.description_en: Industrial raising agents that release carbon dioxide and ammonia during baking. They are commonly used in dry biscuits and crackers. Health: Poorly baked or heavily dosed products may retain an unpleasant ammonia odor and cause irritation, but normal baked use is not considered a major health risk.

entries.name: magnesium carbonates
entries.description_en: Refined magnesium salts used to prevent clumping, regulate acidity, or improve powder flow. Health: Large magnesium doses can cause diarrhea and abdominal cramping; food-additive quantities are usually much lower.

entries.name: hydrochloric acid
entries.description_en: A strong processing acid used in controlled amounts to adjust pH or manufacture ingredients. It is neutralized or highly diluted in the finished food. Health: The concentrated industrial chemical is corrosive, but that hazard should not be confused with properly controlled residues in food.

entries.name: potassium chloride
entries.description_en: A refined mineral salt used to replace sodium, control flavor, or support texture. Health: Excess potassium can cause dangerous heart-rhythm problems in people with kidney disease or certain medications. Normal consumers usually tolerate food amounts.

entries.name: calcium chloride
entries.description_en: A refined calcium salt used to firm vegetables, set cheese, and stabilize texture. Health: High concentrations can irritate the digestive tract and taste bitter, but normal authorized use is not considered a major health concern.

entries.name: magnesium chloride
entries.description_en: A refined magnesium salt used in tofu, mineral fortification, and texture control. Health: Large amounts may cause diarrhea, nausea, or abdominal cramping, especially in people with reduced kidney function.

entries.name: stannous chloride
entries.description_en: A tin compound used mainly to preserve color in a limited number of canned foods. It requires strict concentration limits. Health: Excess inorganic tin can cause acute nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. This is the principal established health concern.

entries.name: sulfuric acid
entries.description_en: A strong industrial acid used in controlled food processing and pH adjustment. It is neutralized or diluted before the food is consumed. Health: Concentrated sulfuric acid is severely corrosive, but properly manufactured food should not retain that corrosive hazard.

entries.name: sodium sulfates
entries.description_en: Refined sulfate salts used in processing and acidity control. Health: Large sulfate doses can draw water into the intestine and cause diarrhea. Sodium-containing forms also add to total sodium intake.

entries.name: potassium sulfates
entries.description_en: Refined potassium salts used to regulate acidity or support processing. Health: People with kidney disease must avoid excessive potassium because it can disturb heart rhythm.

entries.name: calcium sulfate
entries.description_en: A mineral ingredient also known as food-grade gypsum, used for firming, flour treatment, and tofu production. Health: Very high intake can cause digestive discomfort or unnecessarily increase calcium exposure; normal food use is generally low risk.

entries.name: ammonium sulfate
entries.description_en: An industrial salt used in flour treatment, fermentation, and acidity control. Health: No major specific harm is established at permitted levels. Excessive quantities may irritate the digestive system.

entries.name: aluminum sulfate
entries.description_en: An aluminum-containing processing salt used in limited applications. It contributes to total dietary aluminum exposure. Health: Because aluminum can accumulate, repeated exposure from many sources may push intake above the tolerable weekly level, especially in people with reduced kidney function.

entries.name: sodium aluminum sulfate
entries.description_en: An aluminum- and sodium-containing industrial salt used in some baking powders and processing applications. Health: It increases cumulative aluminum and sodium exposure. Frequent consumption of several aluminum-containing products is the main concern.
keywords: sulfate d aluminium et de sodium

entries.name: potassium aluminum sulfate
entries.description_en: Also called potassium alum, this compound is used as a firming or processing agent and adds aluminum to the diet. Health: Long-term concern relates to cumulative aluminum exposure, not an immediate poisoning effect from a single serving.
keywords: sulfate d aluminium et de potassium

entries.name: ammonium aluminum sulfate
entries.description_en: An aluminum-containing industrial salt used for firming or processing in limited foods. Health: Repeated intake contributes to total aluminum exposure, which is limited because the metal can accumulate in the body.
keywords: sulfate d aluminium et d ammonium

entries.name: sodium hydroxide
entries.description_en: A powerful alkaline processing agent used for pretzels, olives, cocoa, and pH control. It is consumed only after reaction, neutralization, washing, or dilution. Health: The concentrated chemical is corrosive. Correct processing must prevent caustic residues in the final food.

entries.name: potassium hydroxide
entries.description_en: A strong alkali used to adjust pH or manufacture other ingredients. It is neutralized or highly diluted during food processing. Health: The raw chemical can cause severe burns, but properly controlled food use should not retain this corrosive effect.

entries.name: calcium hydroxide
entries.description_en: Also known as slaked lime, it is used to firm foods, process corn, and regulate acidity. Health: Concentrated material is irritating and alkaline. Excess residues could irritate the mouth or digestive tract, so processing controls are essential.

entries.name: ammonium hydroxide
entries.description_en: An ammonia solution used in controlled processing and pH adjustment. Most ammonia is removed, reacted, or present at very low residual levels. Health: High residual concentrations would irritate the eyes, airways, and digestive tract and produce a strong odor.

entries.name: magnesium hydroxide
entries.description_en: A refined magnesium compound used to regulate acidity. At larger medicinal doses it also acts as a laxative. Health: Too much can cause diarrhea, cramping, and magnesium accumulation in people with kidney impairment.

entries.name: calcium oxide
entries.description_en: Also called quicklime, it is a highly reactive industrial material used in controlled processing. It reacts to form less aggressive calcium compounds. Health: The raw powder is corrosive and can burn tissue. Finished food must not contain unsafe unreacted residues.

entries.name: magnesium oxide
entries.description_en: A refined magnesium compound used to prevent clumping or regulate acidity. Health: Large doses may cause diarrhea or magnesium accumulation, particularly in people with impaired kidney function.

entries.name: sodium ferrocyanide
entries.description_en: A stable iron-cyanide complex used in salt to prevent clumping. It is not the same as free cyanide under normal food conditions. Health: Current authorized uses are low. Purity and compliance with exposure limits are more relevant than the alarming chemical name.

entries.name: potassium ferrocyanide
entries.description_en: A stable anti-caking complex used mainly in salt. It does not normally release dangerous free cyanide during ordinary food use. Health: The additive should still remain within regulatory limits and purity specifications.

entries.name: calcium ferrocyanide
entries.description_en: A stable mineral complex used to keep salt and powders free-flowing. Health: No major safety concern is established at authorized use levels. The principal controls are dose and chemical purity.

entries.name: sodium aluminum phosphate, acidic
entries.description_en: An acidic aluminum salt used in some baking powders and bakery products to control gas release. Health: It adds both aluminum and sodium. Heavy reliance on products containing aluminum additives can increase total exposure above recommended limits.
keywords: phosphate d'aluminium et de sodium acide

entries.name: silicon dioxide
entries.description_en: A finely divided mineral powder used to prevent clumping and improve flow in seasonings, powders, and supplements. Health: Current authorized food uses are not considered a general safety concern, but particle characterization and metal impurities require strict specifications.

entries.name: calcium silicate
entries.description_en: A mineral anti-caking agent used in dry powders. Modern long-term toxicology data have been insufficient for a fully updated safety conclusion. Health: The concern is incomplete evidence on repeated exposure, not a proven disease effect at ordinary food levels.

entries.name: magnesium silicate
entries.description_en: A processed mineral used to keep powders dry and free-flowing. The available modern data are limited for a complete long-term assessment. Health: Use should remain controlled because chronic exposure has not been characterized as thoroughly as for better-studied additives.

entries.name: magnesium trisilicate
entries.description_en: A mineral anti-caking compound used in powdered foods. Its long-term safety database is incomplete. Health: The concern is uncertainty from limited chronic and reproductive data, rather than confirmed toxicity from normal food use.

entries.name: talc
entries.description_en: Food-grade talc is used to prevent sticking or clumping. Safety depends strongly on mineral purity, particle properties, and the absence of asbestos contamination. Health: Contaminated talc would be unacceptable and potentially harmful. Only material meeting strict food-grade purity standards should be used.

entries.name: sodium aluminum silicate
entries.description_en: An industrial anti-caking mineral that also contributes aluminum. The toxicology database has not supported a fully conclusive modern assessment. Health: Cumulative aluminum exposure and incomplete long-term data are the main reasons for concern.

entries.name: potassium aluminum silicate
entries.description_en: An aluminum-containing mineral used to improve powder flow. It adds to aluminum exposure and has limited modern toxicology data. Health: Frequent intake from several aluminum-containing foods may increase total exposure, especially for vulnerable consumers.

entries.name: fatty acids
entries.description_en: Refined fatty acids used as processing aids, glazing agents, or anti-caking agents. The E-number does not identify a single harmful fat. Health: Health impact depends more on the source and overall fat profile of the food than on this additive function.

entries.name: gluconic acid
entries.description_en: An organic acid produced from glucose and used to regulate acidity or bind minerals. Health: It has low toxicity, although concentrated or high amounts may irritate the digestive system.

entries.name: glucono-delta-lactone
entries.description_en: A glucose-derived compound that slowly releases gluconic acid, helping set tofu, cure foods, and control acidity. Health: Large amounts may cause bloating, gas, or digestive discomfort.

entries.name: sodium gluconate
entries.description_en: A refined sodium salt used to bind metals, stabilize products, and control acidity. Health: Its main nutritional concern is added sodium rather than specific toxicity.

entries.name: potassium gluconate
entries.description_en: A potassium salt used for mineral fortification and product stability. Health: Excess potassium can be dangerous for people with kidney disease or medicines that impair potassium removal.

entries.name: calcium gluconate
entries.description_en: A calcium salt used for firming, fortification, and stabilization. Health: Very high calcium intake can cause constipation and may be unsuitable for people with certain kidney or calcium-balance disorders.

entries.name: ferrous gluconate
entries.description_en: An iron salt used to darken olives and provide iron. It can significantly increase iron exposure in concentrated products. Health: Excess iron can cause nausea, constipation, abdominal pain, and oxidative injury. It is especially dangerous in large accidental doses to children.

entries.name: ferrous lactate
entries.description_en: An iron salt used mainly to stabilize the dark color of olives and other foods. Health: Too much iron may cause digestive symptoms and is unsuitable for people with iron-overload disorders.

entries.name: 4-hexylresorcinol
entries.description_en: A synthetic anti-browning agent used mainly on crustaceans to slow discoloration. Current use is narrow and residue-controlled. Health: No major concern is established at authorized residues. Broader or higher exposure would require additional safety evidence.

entries.name: argon
entries.description_en: An inert gas used to displace oxygen and slow oxidation in packaged food and beverages. Health: It does not react significantly with food and is not considered a safety concern in authorized packaging use.

entries.name: helium
entries.description_en: An inert gas used in specialized packaging or processing. It leaves no meaningful chemical residue in food. Health: Food use is not considered a safety concern. Inhalation of pressurized helium is a separate non-food hazard.

entries.name: oxygen
entries.description_en: A natural gas used in controlled-atmosphere packaging and processing. Health: It is not toxic at food-packaging exposure. It can accelerate oxidation, rancidity, and vitamin loss in some foods.

entries.name: hydrogen
entries.description_en: A gas used in limited food-processing applications. It is highly flammable during industrial handling but does not remain as a toxic food residue. Health: The main hazard is fire or explosion during manufacturing, not consumption of properly processed food.

entries.name: xylitol
entries.description_en: A sugar alcohol used to replace sugar in chewing gum, candy, drinks, and low-sugar products. It is highly refined and can cause gas, abdominal cramps, bloating, or diarrhea when a large amount is consumed. Health: The main established concern is a dose-related laxative effect. People with irritable bowel syndrome or sensitivity to polyols may react at lower amounts.

entries.name: erythritol
entries.description_en: A fermented and purified sugar alcohol used as a low-calorie sweetener. Large single doses can cause diarrhea, nausea, bloating, or abdominal discomfort. Health: EFSA confirmed a laxative threshold. Studies have reported cardiovascular associations, but a causal health risk from normal food consumption has not been established.

entries.name: polyvinylpolypyrrolidone (pvpp)
entries.description_en: A synthetic, insoluble polymer used to clarify beverages or stabilize supplements. It is poorly absorbed from the digestive tract. Health: Safety depends on strict limits for residual monomers and manufacturing impurities.

entries.name: polyvinyl alcohol (pva)
entries.description_en: A synthetic polymer used in edible films, coatings, and supplement capsules. It is only partly absorbed and is used for a technological purpose. Health: The principal concern is product purity and residual manufacturing chemicals rather than a proven toxic effect at permitted levels.

entries.name: pullulan
entries.description_en: A fermentation-produced carbohydrate polymer used to make edible films, capsules, and coatings. Health: Several grams at once may cause abdominal fullness, gas, bloating, or cramps in some people.

entries.name: basic methacrylate copolymer
entries.description_en: A synthetic polymer used mainly to coat food supplements and control how tablets dissolve. Health: It is poorly absorbed. Safety relies on low residual monomers, controlled purity, and restricted use.

entries.name: oxidized starch
entries.description_en: Starch chemically modified to improve thickening, stability, and processing performance. It is used to engineer consistent texture in sauces, fillings, and processed foods. Health: No specific major toxicity is established at authorized levels. It is primarily a marker of industrial formulation.

entries.name: phosphated distarch phosphate
entries.description_en: A cross-linked and phosphorylated starch designed to resist heat, acid, and mechanical processing. Health: It has no established carcinogenic classification. Its role is technological rather than nutritional.

entries.name: hydroxypropyl starch
entries.description_en: A chemically modified starch that remains stable during freezing, heating, and storage. Health: No major specific harm is established at permitted use. Frequent presence indicates a highly engineered texture.

entries.name: acetylated oxidized starch
entries.description_en: A starch subjected to oxidation and acetylation to improve stability, clarity, and texture. Health: It is not classified as carcinogenic. The main issue is its use as a structural ingredient in heavily processed products.

entries.name: triethyl citrate
entries.description_en: A manufactured citrate ester used as a carrier, solvent, or plasticizer for flavors and coatings. Health: No major specific harm is established at authorized levels. Total exposure should remain within the acceptable daily intake.

entries.name: glyceryl diacetate (diacetin)
entries.description_en: A manufactured glycerol ester used to carry flavors, retain moisture, and improve processing. Health: It is broken down into glycerol and acetic acid. Modern long-term data are less extensive than for some common additives, but no major risk is established at permitted use.

entries.name: benzyl alcohol
entries.description_en: An aromatic alcohol used mainly as a solvent or carrier in flavorings. Food exposure is limited, but it is biologically active at high doses. Health: Large systemic doses can depress the nervous system and disturb metabolism. Newborns are particularly vulnerable to high medicinal exposure, although food amounts are far lower.

entries.name: propylene glycol
entries.description_en: A synthetic solvent and moisture-retaining agent used in flavors, colors, enzymes, and processed foods. It is not the same substance as toxic ethylene glycol. Health: Very high exposure can cause hyperosmolality, lactic acidosis, nervous-system depression, and kidney stress, especially in infants or people with impaired liver or kidney function.
